title: Under Pontius Pilate (CCC 595–598)
hookLine: the Church teaches that Jews are not collectively responsible for his death; all sinners share it

lines: A ROMAN OFFICIAL IN THE CREED.
cards: In the middle of the Creed, between the words about God and the words about eternity, there's a Roman official. Suffered under Pontius Pilate. A provincial governor, named in a profession of faith.
Some readers hear his name as a pin in a map: this happened in a real place, under a real government, at a real time. But his name raises a harder question too, one the Catechism doesn't dodge.
Who is responsible for the death of Jesus? Christians have given terrible answers to that question, and the Catechism says so.

teach.h: A TANGLED STORY, A ROMAN CROSS.
teach.b: Day sixty-three stood before Pilate; now, the harder question.

The Gospels tell a tangled story: a betrayal by a friend, some of the religious authorities in Jerusalem, a crowd stirred up in the moment, and a governor who finds no cause, washes his hands, and hands Jesus over anyway.
Crucifixion was a Roman punishment, and Rome carried it out. The trial's history is complex, the Catechism says, and the personal guilt of each person involved is known to God alone.

teach.h: NOT THE JEWS AS A WHOLE.
teach.b: The responsibility, it says, cannot be laid on the Jews of Jerusalem as a whole.
It quotes the Second Vatican Council: what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, without distinction, nor against the Jews of today.
And Jews are not to be spoken of as rejected or accursed, as if scripture taught it.
Then the Catechism turns the question around, quoting the older Roman Catechism: sinners were the authors and ministers of all the sufferings Christ endured. All sinners.
So, it says, Christians themselves carry the gravest share, and it admits that Christians have all too often laid that burden on the Jews alone. A confession, written into a book of teaching.
At the center is the man on the cross, who in Luke's Gospel prays for the people killing him.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do."
So the Creed's phrase keeps two things together: a real governor in a real province, and a death that, in Catholic teaching, belongs to no single people, because every sinner has a hand in it.

how: Catholics profess "suffered under Pontius Pilate" in the Creed, and Catholic teaching, following the Second Vatican Council, rejects blaming the Jewish people for the death of Jesus.

o: the Creed's anchor in a real time and place

p: found no cause, and handed him over

the Catechism, quoting Vatican II, rejects that outright.

suffered under Pontius Pilate: a real governor, in a profession of faith.

games.q: you're Pilate. you find no cause in him, but the crowd is growing loud. what do you do?
o: wash your hands and hand him over
games.why: Matthew says Pilate washed his hands before the people and handed Jesus over to be crucified. the Creed still names him.

practice: Let a group of people come to mind that you sometimes lump together, by religion, country, politics or neighborhood, and notice the shortcut sentence that comes with them, the one that starts with they all.
Then picture one real person from that group, a face and a name, and see which is truer, the shortcut or the person. If you pray, you can use the words from the cross: Father, forgive them.
